title: Why You Should Never Praise Students For Altruism altruism/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin makes a psychological argument against the common practice of loudly praising students for acts of kindness. He contends that external praise cheapens intrinsically rewarding acts, teaching students to expect payment for kindness and gradually extinguishing the internal satisfaction that made the behavior worth doing in the first place. He extends the argument to happiness generally, claiming that a sense of being a benefit to others is deeply satisfying on its own, and that praise dilutes that satisfaction while training students to chase external validation instead of their own values — a pattern he links to broader social-media-driven approval-seeking. His prescription is not to withhold all praise but to redirect it: praise should be aimed at students' work and effort relative to their own prior performance, not at their character or kindness, so it functions as clear, honest feedback rather than manipulation or flattery.
points: Praising students for kind acts actually discourages future altruism by turning an intrinsically rewarding act into something done for external payment.
External praise for kindness teaches students to look around for recognition instead of feeling the natural satisfaction of helping.
Chasing external validation instead of one's own values is described as a broader, culture-wide problem worsened by social media and gaming.
Praise should still be given, but directed at students' work and effort relative to their own past performance, not at their character.
Effective praise functions as honest feedback that shows students what success looks like, without flattery or exaggeration.
quotes: But it’s a mistake. It’s a mistake that actually discourages altruistic behavior. Keep praising and you’ll see less of it, not more.
Our sense of empathy dampens when we receive something external in return for our kind acts. Because, you see, payment in any form weakens the moment’s intrinsic value.
Praise over time effectively removes the joy of helping others.
Many students nowadays have been praised and rewarded so much that they’re all but dead inside, chasing hits of dopamine from social media and video games.
Praise is something you give as a form of feedback in response to new learning, effort, or achievement beyond what your students have done before.
It’s honest and worthy and done to communicate and define what is good and in their best interest.
